questions.q: Why does documentation written only for your own memory tend to fail when someone else reads it?
options: It assumes context the reader doesn't have, since it was written for someone who already knew every decision
It is always too short to be useful
Other engineers are not allowed to read personal notes
It fails only if it contains spelling errors
questions.explain: Notes written for yourself, in the moment, skip the background a reader without your context actually needs.

questions.q: What is the key difference this lesson draws between documenting WHAT was configured and WHY it was configured?
options: WHAT records the fact (e.g. the CIDR block); WHY explains the reasoning behind choosing it, which is what lets a future engineer reason about the decision later
WHAT and WHY are two words for the same thing in good documentation
WHY is only relevant for security-related configuration
WHAT is always more important to document than WHY
questions.explain: A fact alone ('Subnet: 10.0.1.0/24') tells a reader less than the fact plus the reasoning behind it (room for 3x growth).

questions.q: In the subnet example, why was a /24 chosen over a /28?
options: To leave room for growth, since the team expected roughly 3x the current VM count within a year
Because /28 blocks are not supported by any cloud provider
Because a /24 is always required by compliance regulations
There was no reason given — the choice was arbitrary
questions.explain: The documented rationale was growth headroom, since resizing a live subnet later is disruptive.

questions.q: What is the 'new-hire test' described in this lesson?
options: Imagining a new hire with no access to you, reading only what you wrote, and asking whether they could understand and operate around the decision without messaging you
A quiz given to every new employee on their first day
A requirement that documentation be reviewed by HR before publishing
A test that only applies to monitoring thresholds, not other decisions
questions.explain: The new-hire test checks whether documentation is self-sufficient: if you can picture the question they'd have to ask, that question belongs in the document.

questions.q: Besides subnet sizing, what other examples does this lesson say the WHAT-vs-WHY distinction applies to?
options: VM sizing choices, backup retention windows, and monitoring thresholds
Only billing and invoicing decisions
Only decisions made by senior engineers
It applies to no other examples — subnet sizing is a special case
questions.explain: The lesson extends the same principle to VM sizing, backup retention, and monitoring thresholds, where the WHY is expected growth, a compliance need, or a past incident.
